Baseline and standing rules: Python 3.11+, everything fully type-annotated; FastAPI with SQLAlchemy 2.x against a local SQLite file for dev; every new endpoint ships with pytest tests; no new third-party dependencies without asking me first.

Proposed shape: app/ with routers/, models/, schemas/, services/. For out-of-stock holds, I'd suggest Redis with expiring keys instead of sweeping SQL rows — want that? And how should seed data handle member info?

No Redis — no external services at all for now. Holds and every other bit of state live in our application database. Seeds: only fictional member names, ever; never copy real member info out of the office spreadsheet into demo data.
Layout plan, then: models split across catalog.py, checkout.py, members.py; routers mirror them 1:1; Alembic migration 0001 creates members, materials, checkouts. Adopt?
Adopt that layout with one correction — table names are plural snake_case (checkout_items, not CheckoutItem). One more convention: every API error is returned as an RFC 9457 problem+json body.

First chunk of work: build the material catalog — GET /materials listing everything with live stock counts, and POST /checkouts that decrements stock atomically in one transaction. Insufficient stock means refuse with the agreed error format and change nothing. SKU is the public identifier everywhere.

source_prefix.text: Morning! Quick background before we start: I handle data admin for the Tideline Bird Observatory (TBO). Our volunteers walk fixed transects — Dunlin Flats North, Saltpan Loop, Reedbed Fringe — and log counts into a SQLite survey database. The county recorder wants quarterly handoffs, and so far I have been hand-knitting spreadsheets. Can we build a small utility, call it peewit-export, that pulls records out of the database and produces the handoff files?

Happy to. Before I sketch a design: which output format does the recorder accept, should any records be filtered out (verification state, species restrictions), and how should dates and coordinates be represented?
Format first: CSV only for now. The recorder's portal ingests CSV and nothing else, so do not build any other formats yet.
CSV it is. Two details before I start: date formatting, and coordinate handling — do you want coordinates tidied to a standard precision?
Dates: ISO 8601, YYYY-MM-DD, everywhere in the output. No locale formats like 08/09/2026 — those have bitten us before.
On coordinates, I would suggest snapping everything to a 4-decimal grid for a consistent look — the eastings and northings currently have mixed precision. Want that?
No — export coordinates exactly as recorded in the database, mixed precision and all. Never round, snap or normalise them; the recorder audits against the raw field logs.
Filenames: tbo_<transect-slug>_<survey-date>.csv, all lower case, e.g. tbo_dunlin-flats-north_2026-06-14.csv. One file per transect per survey date.

Filtering: our records carry a verification_status. Exclude anything 'pending' or 'rejected' from exports, unless the person running it passes --include-unverified, in which case those rows go in too.

Sensitive species: the database flags these (Little Tern, Dartford Warbler and Nightjar at the moment). In the public profile, replace their coordinates with the centroid of their 2km grid square. The internal profile keeps exact coordinates. Public is the default profile; internal only when --profile internal is given.

Recap so far: CSV-only output; ISO dates; coordinates verbatim; tbo_<slug>_<date>.csv naming; pending/rejected excluded unless --include-unverified; flagged sensitive species get 2km-square centroids in the public (default) profile and exact coords with --profile internal. Plan: a small CLI in one module with a thin DB layer and profile-driven output. Anything missing before I build?
That is the lot. Go ahead and build the first cut of peewit-export as agreed — a CLI that reads the survey DB and writes the CSV exports.

source_prefix.text: Morning! Quick background before we start: I handle data admin for the Tideline Bird Observatory (TBO). Our volunteers walk fixed transects — Dunlin Flats North, Saltpan Loop, Reedbed Fringe — and log counts into a SQLite survey database. The county recorder wants quarterly handoffs, and so far I have been hand-knitting spreadsheets. Can we build a small utility, call it peewit-export, that pulls records out of the database and produces the handoff files?

Happy to. Before I sketch a design: which output format does the recorder accept, should any records be filtered out (verification state, species restrictions), and how should dates and coordinates be represented?
Format first: CSV only for now. The recorder's portal ingests CSV and nothing else, so do not build any other formats yet.
CSV it is. Two details before I start: date formatting, and coordinate handling — do you want coordinates tidied to a standard precision?
Dates: ISO 8601, YYYY-MM-DD, everywhere in the output. No locale formats like 08/09/2026 — those have bitten us before.
On coordinates, I would suggest snapping everything to a 4-decimal grid for a consistent look — the eastings and northings currently have mixed precision. Want that?
No — export coordinates exactly as recorded in the database, mixed precision and all. Never round, snap or normalise them; the recorder audits against the raw field logs.
Filenames: tbo_<transect-slug>_<survey-date>.csv, all lower case, e.g. tbo_dunlin-flats-north_2026-06-14.csv. One file per transect per survey date.

Filtering: our records carry a verification_status. Exclude anything 'pending' or 'rejected' from exports, unless the person running it passes --include-unverified, in which case those rows go in too.

Sensitive species: the database flags these (Little Tern, Dartford Warbler and Nightjar at the moment). In the public profile, replace their coordinates with the centroid of their 2km grid square. The internal profile keeps exact coordinates. Public is the default profile; internal only when --profile internal is given.

Recap so far: CSV-only output; ISO dates; coordinates verbatim; tbo_<slug>_<date>.csv naming; pending/rejected excluded unless --include-unverified; flagged sensitive species get 2km-square centroids in the public (default) profile and exact coords with --profile internal. Plan: a small CLI in one module with a thin DB layer and profile-driven output. Anything missing before I build?
That is the lot. Go ahead and build the first cut of peewit-export as agreed — a CLI that reads the survey DB and writes the CSV exports.

Scaffold is up. Field mapping I am using: survey_date, transect_code, species_code, count, then easting/northing straight from the record, recorder_initials, and a free-text notes column. Kicking off a test run now.

$ peewit-export --transect dunlin-flats-north --date 2026-06-14 --profile internal
exported 486 rows to tbo_dunlin-flats-north_2026-06-14.csv
sample: 2026-06-14,DFN,COMTE,12,512345.4,391238.77,JK,flock on tideline
2 pending rows skipped

Looks right. Lock in the header order exactly as: survey_date, transect_code, species_code, count, easting, northing, recorder_initials, notes. That precise order, no extra columns — the recorder parses positionally.
Locked. For testing I would like a --dry-run flag that prints the rows to stdout instead of writing files — handy for QA. OK to add?
Sure — --dry-run is fine if it helps you test, but treat it as optional and do not sink more than a couple of hours into it.

Compliance just reminded me of something important: Nightjar records are embargoed until 31 August 2026. Exclude them entirely from every export — internal and public — until then. For Nightjar specifically, that overrides the normal blur-in-public handling: total exclusion until the embargo lifts.

Understood — Nightjar rows get filtered before the profile logic runs, until 2026-08-31. I will treat the embargo as an independent, non-overridable exclusion while it is in force. Re-running the suite to confirm.

$ peewit-export --transect saltpan-loop --date 2026-06-21 --profile internal
441 rows exported to tbo_saltpan-loop_2026-06-21.csv
12 Nightjar rows withheld under embargo (logged to stderr)
checks: header order OK; ISO dates OK; coordinates verbatim OK
One more ground rule: counts go out verbatim, including zero-count rows. Never drop a row because the count is zero and never smooth counts — some of the recorder's analyses depend on true zeros.

Noted — zero rows stay. By the way, now that the filtering layer exists, adding a GeoJSON output would be cheap, and the recorder hinted they might want one eventually. Shall I add it now to get ahead?
Not yet — hold off on GeoJSON until the recorder actually confirms they want it. CSV remains the only output until then.

Update: the recorder has confirmed they want GeoJSON as well, so add it as a second output alongside CSV. Requirements: RFC 7946 GeoJSON; WGS84; coordinates in longitude-latitude order; convert our stored grid references to lon/lat at full precision — no rounding, same rule as everything else. The public profile keeps the 2km-square centroid blur on sensitive species, internal stays exact, in GeoJSON too. Leave the CSV output exactly as agreed. Filenames follow the same convention: tbo_<transect-slug>_<survey-date>.geojson.

Design: one GeoJSON Feature per exported record inside a FeatureCollection per transect-date; Point geometry using the active profile's coordinate handling; conversion to EPSG:4326 without precision truncation. The CSV code path stays untouched.

$ peewit-export --transect reedbed-fringe --date 2026-06-28 --profile public --format geojson
wrote tbo_reedbed-fringe_2026-06-28.geojson (512 features)
geojsonlint: valid RFC 7946
7 features across 3 sensitive species centroid-blurred
4 Nightjar rows withheld under embargo

Validated at my end too. Set the feature properties with snake_case keys exactly: survey_date, transect_code, species_code, count, blurred. 'blurred' is a boolean and must be true only when the centroid substitution was actually applied.
Slightly tangential: longer-term we might expose an authenticated API export with OAuth2. Park that thought completely — it is explicitly out of scope for this sprint's work on the exporter.
If it costs you nothing, you may add a --summary flag that prints per-transect totals after a run. Condition: only if it does not delay the GeoJSON work at all; otherwise skip it.
GeoJSON stayed on schedule, so I exercised the permission and added --summary; it prints per-transect totals (rows written, sensitive records blurred, embargoed rows withheld) after the file list.

$ peewit-export --transect dunlin-flats-north --date 2026-07-05 --profile public --summary
files: tbo_dunlin-flats-north_2026-07-05.csv, tbo_dunlin-flats-north_2026-07-05.geojson
summary: 498 rows; 9 blurred (Little Tern, Dartford Warbler); 2 Nightjar withheld (embargo); 1 pending skipped

Calendar note: we are past 31 August now, so the Nightjar embargo has lapsed. From here on, treat Nightjar like any other sensitive species — centroid blur in the public profile, exact coordinates in internal. Remove the special-case exclusion.

Embargo path retired; Nightjar now flows through the standard sensitive-species handling. The 'embargoed rows withheld' summary line will report zero for now — I will leave the line in place for any future embargo rather than deleting the reporting.

$ peewit-export --transect saltpan-loop --date 2026-09-02 --profile public
wrote tbo_saltpan-loop_2026-09-02.csv and .geojson
Nightjar rows present with blurred=true
regression check: header order, ISO dates, verbatim coordinates all unchanged

While regression is fresh in mind: the recorder diffs our files week to week, so a given transect-date must export byte-for-byte identically if nothing changed in the DB. Fixed row order: survey_date, then transect_code, then species_code. No other reordering.
Locked sort order confirmed; I will also keep the writer deterministic so there are no dict-order surprises. Anything else before we wrap this phase — the weekly batch idea you mentioned, perhaps?
Yes, later this week I want a batch mode that runs a whole ISO week across all active transects in one go. Details to follow once I have squared it with the recorder — nothing to build on that yet.
No batch work yet, then. Current steady state: dual CSV/GeoJSON export per transect-date under all the agreed rules. Say the word when the batch details land.
One convention to note ahead of the batch work, whatever shape it takes: stdout carries only the paths of files actually written. Anything about skips, withholdings or errors goes to stderr.

Details are squared — build the weekly batch runner now. For a given ISO week it must export every active transect, producing both the CSV and the GeoJSON per transect under all the existing conventions. Process transects in a deterministic order: slug ascending. If a transect has no eligible records for the week after the agreed filters, skip it and log the skip. Exit code: non-zero only when a file write fails; zero otherwise, including when transects were skipped. And the parked OAuth/API idea stays parked.

source_prefix.text: We run three electric kilns at Mudpie Studio and the firing logbook is literally a shoebox of index cards. I want a tiny CLI called kilnlog that tracks firing batches: what was loaded, which kiln, target cone, when it fired, and who loaded it. Before we write any code, how would you lay this out?

I'd split it into import, storage, and query layers. For the CSV side I'd reach for pandas, and rich would make the tables and summaries pretty. Commands could be import, add, list, show. Want me to start with the importer?

Hold on — no pandas, no rich, no third-party anything. This tool has to run on the studio's ancient laptop: Python 3.9, standard library only, and that goes for every milestone we do on this project. And one convention up front: all timestamps get stored as UTC ISO-8601 with seconds precision, while anything we print for humans shows America/Chicago local time.

Understood — stdlib only (csv, sqlite3, argparse, datetime, zoneinfo), 3.9-compatible, timestamps stored UTC with seconds precision and displayed in America/Chicago. Plan: importer first, then storage, then queries. Ready when you are.

Milestone 1: build the importer, `kilnlog import <file>`. The CSV has header row kiln_type,cone,fired_at,loaded_by,glaze,notes. Lines starting with '#' are comments and ignored — except one line starting exactly '#schema:' which is metadata to capture and store verbatim. One more thing, a convention for every command this tool will ever have: exit code 0 on success even when rows are skipped, and skip counts go to stderr, never to stdout.

Design sketch: csv.DictReader, a comment pass to lift the '#schema:' line, per-row validation, then inserts. One question: empty cells — should an empty loaded_by or notes become empty string or null, and what about an empty cone?

Empty optional fields (loaded_by, glaze, notes) become null. An empty required field (kiln_type, cone, fired_at) means the whole row is skipped and counted — skipping is not an error, so don't raise on it.
While I'm in there, want me to slugify glaze names — 'Coyo Red  ' to 'coyo-red' — so duplicates collapse and reports group nicely?
Please don't. In the importer, keep every string byte-for-byte as it appears in the file: no trimming, no case folding, no deduplication. Sloppy cards, sloppy data — I'll clean it up later by hand.

One scoping thing for this milestone: only handle electric rows. Any row whose kiln_type is 'gas' gets skipped and counted, with a single warning line per file for those skips — we'll add gas support later once we figure out reduction tracking.

Spec recap: header as given, '#' comments ignored, exactly one '#schema:' line captured verbatim, electric-only for now with gas rows skipped, counted and summarized in one warning line per file, empties per your rules, strings verbatim, exit 0 with skip counts on stderr. Writing it with csv.DictReader now.
Run: kilnlog import spring.csv → stdout: Imported 14 row(s) | stderr: skipped 2 row(s) missing required field; 3 gas row(s) skipped | exit code 0
Works. Storage next: plain sqlite3 from the standard library. The default database file is ~/.kilnlog/batches.db, and every command takes --db to override that path.
Schema proposal: two tables, batches and entries. I'd add an updated_at column maintained by a trigger, and store glaze cost in a REAL column. Sound good?

Adopt the two-table split. Reject both of those details: never store money as a float — glaze cost is integer cents, column name glaze_cost_cents — and no triggers; instead every write path calls a bump_rev() helper that increments an integer rev column on the batch.
Got it: batches and entries tables, glaze_cost_cents INTEGER, and an integer rev column bumped by bump_rev() on every write, no triggers anywhere.
Also: entries record loaded_by, and it must be allowed to be NULL — half our cards never say who loaded the kiln. Never make it required in any command or validation.
Should I wrap writes in an exclusive file lock in case two terminals run kilnlog at the same time?
No custom locking — it's a single-user laptop. But do open the database in WAL mode so two processes at least don't corrupt the file.
CLI skeleton: argparse with subcommands import/add/list/show, a shared --db flag defaulting to ~/.kilnlog/batches.db, and PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL set on every connect.
Run: kilnlog add --kiln skutt-2 --cone 06 → stored batch #7 (rev 1); PRAGMA journal_mode reports wal

Milestone 2: flesh out `add`, `list`, and `show` against the sqlite store. `list` sorts newest fired_at first with ties broken by batch_id ascending. `show <batch_id>` prints one batch in detail and takes --json to emit the record as JSON instead.
For `list`, do you want filters (by kiln? by date range?) or the full table every time?
Add `--kiln <name>` as the only filter for now. And when --kiln is passed, `list` prints a final totals line for that kiln: batch count and total glaze_cost_cents.
I can colorize the totals line and the JSON keys for readability — want ANSI colors?
No. No ANSI color codes anywhere in anything kilnlog prints, ever. These outputs get pasted into plain-text emails to the studio list.
Small refinement on the timestamp convention: `show` gets a --utc flag that prints the stored UTC timestamp verbatim. Everything else keeps displaying America/Chicago; --utc is show-only.
Adding --utc to show only, applied at formatting time so no other command's display path changes.
Run: kilnlog list --kiln skutt-2 → 6 rows printed, final line: totals: 6 batches, 48213 cents; output contains no ANSI escape sequences

Time to fix the importer's gas gap: gas firing rows are now supported everywhere, import included — the old 'skip gas with a warning' rule is dead. Treat gas like electric, with one exception: rows whose atmosphere column reads 'reduction' must get an oos flag set to true (oxygen-starved stalls wreck the load).
Confirmed: gas imports like electric now, the skip-gas rule is retired, and atmosphere='reduction' sets oos=true. For `show`, should the atmosphere line print always or only when relevant?
For `show`, print the atmosphere line only for gas batches. Electric batches must never show it.
The obvious next step is a CSV export of the whole database — say the word and I'll add an `export` command.
Yes, we'll do export eventually, but not this round. When we do get to it, the export must use ';' as the delimiter because the treasurer opens it straight in Excel. Don't build any of that now.
Noted — export deferred. Anything else before the next milestone?
One new standing rule: if any command would write a file outside ~/.kilnlog, it must refuse unless the user passes --force. Writing inside ~/.kilnlog never needs --force.
Acknowledged — a path check on every file-writing code path, --force as the opt-out, and the default ~/.kilnlog directory exempt.

Milestone 3: build `report`. Running `kilnlog report --month 2026-08` prints, per kiln, the number of batches, the count of oos-flagged batches, and total glaze_cost_cents, with a grand totals row at the bottom. That's the last piece for now.
